title: Motion as information — Image Wiki
text:
Motion as information
  Movement used to tell the reader something — where a thing came from, and that it is still the same thing. Motion is the loudest signal an interface has, which is why spending it on decoration is expensive.

  
    Termpurposeful motion / UI animation
    Also calledUI animation, transitions, microinteractions, motion design
    Not the same asmotion vs decoration, transition vs loading spinner, animation vs video
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        The two jobs motion actually doesWhy it is expensiveDirection and easing are meaning, not polishWhat motion cannot doCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Tap a row in a list and a full-screen panel appears. Now tap a different row in a different app and the panel grows out of the row you touched. Same information, same two screens. In the second one you never wonder what you are looking at.
That is the whole subject. Motion is not a finish; it is a channel that carries two specific facts and almost nothing else.



Eadweard Muybridge, The Horse in Motion ("Sallie Gardner", Palo Alto track, 19 June 1878). Library of Congress; public domain.
Read the printed note under the plate: the negatives were made "at intervals of twenty-seven inches of distance, and about the twenty-fifth part of a second of time". Twelve frames, forty milliseconds apart, of one stride.
This is what a motion specification looks like — then and now. Nobody can argue about a movement while watching it at speed, so you stop it, lay the instants side by side, and check them one at a time. The vertical lines are 27 inches apart and the horizontals four inches, so you can measure the horse rather than admire it.


The two jobs motion actually does
Causality. A thing that grows out of the row you touched has visible parentage. You do not have to work out where the panel came from, or which of the nine things on screen produced it, because you watched it happen. NN/g calls this the difference between an animation that is a "clue about what is currently happening with the system" and one that is time-filling visual stimulation (MOTION-007).
Continuity. A change of state normally destroys the old screen and builds a new one. Motion lets you assert that some object survived the change — this panel is that row, the list is still underneath, you have not gone anywhere. That assertion matters because when it is missing, people reach for the Back button to close an overlay and leave the page instead (MOTION-007).

12345Cutframes 2 to 5 are identical: the panel is simply there12345Shared elementthe tapped row is the same object in every frame, growing into the panel

The same change, storyboarded twice. Top: frames 2 to 5 are identical, because a cut has no in-between — the panel simply exists, and nothing in the picture says which row produced it.
Bottom: the accent block is the same object in all five frames. It starts as a row in the list and ends as the panel, and the siblings fade rather than vanish, so the list is still the place you came from. Note that the interesting information is in frames 2 to 4, which last around a fifth of a second in real time and which nobody consciously looks at.


Everything else people try to do with motion — establish a brand tone, add delight, fill a wait — is either a side effect or a cost.
Why it is expensive
Your visual system is built to catch movement, and it is particularly tuned to motion that looks alive. NN/g grounds this in Pratt and colleagues' 2010 finding that animate motion captures visual attention, and draws the practical conclusion: animation can make a subtle signifier obvious, or it can hijack attention (MOTION-007).
A cart badge that silently ticks from 2 to 3 gets missed, because people do not notice small static changes far from where they were looking; animating it makes the feedback land. The same power, pointed at a flashing countdown clock that expires "in under an hour" no matter when you arrive, is a dark pattern (MOTION-007).
There is a quieter cost too: motion competes with itself. In NN/g's loading-screen example five animations run at once, and "the power of any of these animations to pull the user's attention is diminished by competition from all the others" (MOTION-007). Attention is the budget, and every decorative movement spends some.
Carbon states the consequence as a test question: "The best interface motion may go unnoticed… Is your motion frequently noticed by average users? If so, consider removing or minimizing it" (MOTION-005). Motion you can describe afterwards is usually motion that was too big.
Direction and easing are meaning, not polish



Étienne-Jules Marey, Chronophotograph of a Man on a Bicycle, c. 1885–1890. National Gallery of Art; CC0.
One plate, one rider, five exposures, and you read it instantly as a single man moving right — not as five men. That is continuity doing its work in a still image: same white jacket, same cap, same wheel, in a row.
The spacing is the other half. The gaps between the figures are near enough equal, which tells you the speed was steady. Later in this section that spacing becomes the diagnostic: unequal gaps mean acceleration, and acceleration is what an easing curve is.


Which way something moves is a claim about what it is. A card that rises from the bottom edge says it can be pushed back down; one that slides in from the right invites a swipe back to the right (MOTION-007). Get the direction wrong and you have taught a gesture that does not work.
Easing makes a similar claim about permanence. Carbon reserves its exit curve — where the element speeds up as it goes — for removals, because accelerating away implies the departure "is permanent". A side panel that will be needed again gets the standard curve instead, so that it slows as it leaves and reads as coming to rest just outside the frame (MOTION-005).

screen edgeevery 60 msbiggest step lastAccelerates outgone for good: dismissed, deleted, sentscreen edgeevery 60 msbiggest step firstDecelerates to restparked just outside: a panel you can call back

Same panel, same distance, same 240 ms. Only the spacing of the samples differs, and the ruler under each screen is the thing to read: equal steps in time, unequal steps in space.
Left, the gaps grow, so the panel is still gaining speed when it crosses the edge — it is going somewhere, and it is gone. Right, the gaps shrink to nothing at the edge, so the panel has parked: it is just out of sight and you expect to be able to fetch it back. Nobody has to be told this. It is how thrown things and pushed things behave.


What motion cannot do

It cannot be re-read. A static layout will sit there while you check it twice. A 200 ms transition happens once, at a moment when the reader is looking somewhere else, and there is no way to scroll back. Anything that must be understood belongs in the static state, not in the transition.
It competes with reading. Movement anywhere on the page pulls the eye off the line of text. This is why a moving decoration next to an article is not neutral.
On a slow device it is just a delay. Carbon says it plainly: not all devices are powerful enough to run the motion smoothly, "no matter how essential the motion design is", so always provide an alternative and "make sure there is always a way to communicate similar messages statically" (MOTION-005).
Some people cannot have it at all. Interaction-triggered animation has to be switchable off unless it is essential (MOTION-010). If your explanation lives in the animation, those readers lose the explanation — see Timing and restraint.

Common mistakes

"Animation makes the interface feel polished." It makes it feel polished for about three viewings. After that the only motion people tolerate is motion that told them something. NN/g's usability-test participants were actively frustrated by down-time animations (MOTION-007).
"A spinner is feedback." A spinner says the system is busy. It does not say what will appear, or where. A skeleton placeholder in the shape of the coming content says both (MOTION-007).
"Motion can replace navigation." It cannot. A zoom that implies going deeper is a useful supplement to clear labels, not a substitute for them (MOTION-007).
"Any movement is better than a jump." A cut is a legitimate choice, and the right one when nothing needs explaining. Material's physics system exists so that motion follows one consistent set of rules across a product, not so that every change gets a performance (MOTION-001).


Judging motion in five seconds

Ask what fact the movement asserts. "This came from that", or "this is still the same thing" — if neither, it is decoration.
Freeze it halfway. If the mid-transition frame is nonsense, the transition is doing something the layout cannot support.
Watch the direction. Does it match the gesture that dismisses the thing?
Watch it ten times. Anything still charming at ten will survive being seen forty times a day.
Turn it off in your head. If the interface stops being understandable, the explanation was in the wrong place.
